title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with prices on everything: a bed, a boxed meal, a phone, a lawyer's fee. Those who don't pay stay for years, sometimes more than a decade.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who raise prices on the spot — is the part that's actually worth something.
who: Founders and going-global operators interested in the situation of overseas Chinese, the Philippine business environment, and the machinery of gray industry and immigration corruption.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — surfing history and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: Immigration opens at 1.5 million pesos for immediate release
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, immigration people pulled him aside and said quietly, "I can help you." After the lawyer communicated, the feedback was: give 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can walk out immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people picked up in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing still existed in 2026 and wanted to resolve it through normal legal process. But the price of refusing was this: they were moved from the holding cell at the General City police station to the Immigration Bureau detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When the phone was taken, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was confiscated, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code and his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay — were the same. For the next four or five days he applied however he could and never got the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and the lawyer, and the phone was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but the night before he got the phone back, it had been transferred back in. There was only about 1,000 RMB in there. Feili said it wasn't about the amount; it was that the phone had been touched while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese doing gray-industry scams in Manila go through this same layer of plunder after being arrested, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones hold a mass of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout immigration promised exist — in another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own tickets to transfer, immigration takes turns working on them, saying the Manila immigration facility is very good, has air conditioning, is very free, you can work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying: there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout — just in another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the main detention center past three in the morning. Getting out of the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, iron cages like dog kennels all around, and inside, long communal platforms, several hundred people. Past three in the morning, many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in a pair of underwear, hanging on the iron cages to look at the newcomers. Feili said the few foreigners didn't say a word for several minutes after getting out, then it hit them: immigration had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with immigration, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were newly built by the Chinese boss. Foreigners just stay, but Chinese who come in have to pay. The lowest tier, a communal platform bed, is 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. The wealthy pan bosses and gambling kingpins can pay 50,000 pesos a month, about 6,000-plus, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That is where immigration's earlier claim that "there's air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were all their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, he'd come to serve time, how could he have to pay on top of that. The gang boss, in a threatening tone, said: you're already in here and don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes all food, clothing and daily life for Chinese — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center holds about 200 people; when Feili went in it was the off season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff are paid: the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 pesos. The wages are very low, but many people can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer, so they can only work to earn.

points.h: A Yunnan man held over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken, and he was pulled into a park to do telecom fraud. With poor performance he was shocked with an electric baton by his supervisor every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation process is simple — a few departments sign, you buy your own ticket, and you go — but immigration, in order to extract money, holds you a very long time, and without paying the process doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese uncle got to see the warden. The warden had a guard bring Feili's phone, and had Xiaopang add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterward immigration bought a feature phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese Feili talked with much came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people were surrounded by immigration together with the police and the NBI, three agencies. The first wave of plunder was the NBI and police putting each person in a toilet — because there are no cameras in the toilet — and taking everything valuable off them. The second wave was immigration negotiating with the company boss for people: the quote differed per person, 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the person in charge's mood. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, about 300,000-plus RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food would keep being sent until they got out. This young man ran a book targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; his best month brought in 2 million RMB, and he bought a house and a car in his small home county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, several hundred thousand was transferred away, and a dirty cop pinned an illegal gun-possession charge on him, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: A Philippine lawyer raises the price on the spot when he sees a Chinese client
points.body: In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, about 20,000-plus RMB, done in four weeks. After Feili got to Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying that was the old price and the new price needed another 120,000 pesos, about 10,000-plus RMB. Feili decided not to use him and gave up the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted 30,000-plus RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili said the truly reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedural pipeline extremely well, because everyone held inside is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for 30-plus days, 41 days counting Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.
